query: What drove Jerome to shift away from galaxies as his primary imaging target, and what specific combination of events in Sessions 2 and 3 explains why that shift happened when it did?
gold: Early state (Session 1): Jerome is firmly committed to galaxy work — he has a 10-hour integration plan for M65 and M66 in the Leo Triplet and frames February as 'galaxy season.' Shift signal (Session 3, Turn 6): Jerome announces 'I'm done chasing galaxy targets for this season. Cecilia's nebula images from the 17th actually looked reasonable and I've been reconsidering the target strategy.' The trigger was a combination of two things: (1) repeated transparency failures over February and early March — Jerome describes pulling 12 hours of integration across six nights where 'the transparency killed the faint outer arms every single time,' making his galaxy project unrecoverable; and (2) Cecilia's nebula images from the February session showing him that Ha emission work was viable and delivered results despite those same conditions. Priya had also noted in Session 2 that 'emission nebulae are way more forgiving' with Ha bandpass cutting through poor transparency. The convergence of his own failure and a visible counterexample from Cecilia appears to have tipped him. Evolved state (Session 4 onward): Jerome explicitly commits to emission nebulae — Rosette, Cone, Cygnus Wall — and frames galaxy work as 'simply not compatible with high SNR galaxy work at this latitude.'

His reasoning: narrowband emission work gives consistent results, and the Rosette at 20 hours Ha will be a significantly better image than anything from the galaxy pair. Galaxy season is effectively over for him this year due to transparency variance, so he'll shoot the Rosette and Cone Ha on April 11 regardless.
